extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratology students, and advanced creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classification of narrative modes for rendering character speech and point of view (narratized speech, indirect styles, free indirect style, interior monologue, reported speech) and guidance on focalization/voice distinctions. Useful for close reading, criticism, or crafting narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratized (narrated) speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratized, or narrated, speech is the most distant and generally the most reduced form of representing speech or thought (e.g., "I informed my mother of my decision to marry Albertine" or for thought: "I decided to marry Albertine").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces a brief, event-like statement; closest to 'pure event'. The narrative may, however, develop the inner debate at greater length in an analysis form (a narratized narrative of thoughts). Example: compressing dialogue into a report rather than reproducing it verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposed speech (indirect style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposed speech is rendered in indirect style (e.g., "I told my mother that I absolutely had to marry Albertine" for uttered speech; "I thought that I absolutely had to marry Albertine" for inner speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More mimetic than narrated speech and can be exhaustive in principle, but the narrator's presence is perceptible in the sentence syntax; no guarantee of literal fidelity to the character's original words. The narrator condenses and integrates the speech into his own style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free indirect style
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant where economizing on subordination allows greater extension of the character's speech and a beginning of emancipation from the narrator, often distinguished by the absence of a declarative introductory verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the absent declarative verb, free indirect style can create a double ambiguity: (1) between uttered and inner speech and (2) between the character's speech and the narrator's voice. It is more mimetic than subordinated indirect style but still involves the narrator's integration of the speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported (dramatic/mimetic) speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The most 'mimetic' form: the narrator pretends to give the floor literally to the character (quoted: "I said to my mother: it is absolutely necessary that I marry Albertine"). Historically tied to drama and epic as the basic form of dialogue and monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the character documentary autonomy via quoted speech and vocal imitation. This form has been canonical since Homer and is considered by Plato as superior to narrative report; it foregrounds the character's voice with minimal narrator mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate speech / interior monologue ('immediate' speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech in which the narrating instance is obliterated and the character's ongoing thought-perception-action order takes the foreground from the first lines, often called 'interior monologue' or better 'immediate speech'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator is reduced to silence and the character 'takes the front of the stage.' Works as either an isolated monologue within a narrative (narrator remains in background) or as the mode of a whole narrative (narrator annulled). Examples: Joyce (Molly Bloom), parts of Faulkner; differs fundamentally from free indirect style where the narrator and character voices merge rather than the narrator disappearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing free indirect style from immediate monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal distinction: free indirect style involves the narrator taking on the character's speech (merging instances), whereas immediate monologue obliterates the narrator so the character speaks unaided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect by presence/absence of narrating instance and declarative introductions; free indirect speech keeps a narratorial mediation (even if covert), immediate monologue removes it. Misidentification is common and has aesthetic consequences (e.g., freedom of voice, narrator responsibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradations and blending of speech modes
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice the theoretical types (narratized, transposed/indirect, free indirect, immediate, reported) are rarely cleanly separated and often slide imperceptibly from one to another in actual texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers should attend to subtle transitions (as in Proust) where narrator voice returns or relinquishes control, and to how these gradations shape interpretation of character subjectivity and narrative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported inner speech (Proustian handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic use of reported inner speech where the hero articulates thoughts as a theatrical monologue within narratorial handling—often rhetorically charged rather than 'inchoate' stream-of-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust's inner speeches are traditionally handled (not pure infraverbal flux); they may be lively and rhetorical, and often remain under narrator control for demonstrative aims. Do not confuse rhetorically articulated reported thought with authentic immediate interior monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicity and unreliability of inner speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Inner speech can be oblique, deceitful, or insincere (e.g., characters talking aloud to themselves while masking their true motives), and therefore unfaithful to the 'felt truth' it purports to reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist should show the gap between inner speech and felt truth—expose 'concealments of bad faith'—because inner monologue alone cannot guarantee access to authentic feeling. Use contrasts (insincere monologues, actions, contextual cues) to reveal duplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting infralinguistic or dream-language sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoherent or infralinguistic sequences in dreams or monologues (e.g., 'deer, Francis Jammes, fork') are not evidence of a privileged 'alogical depth' but indicate a rupture between two logics (dream logic vs waking logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such sequences as representational devices that signal misunderstanding or discontinuity between mental states, not as straightforward examples of 'primordial' or 'deep' unconscious speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivization of characters' language (stylistic autonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting linguistic autonomy to characters so that their speech acquires an 'objectivized' status distinct from the narrator's voice—ranges from minimal connotative marks to fully individualized idiolects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique intensifies mimetic effect and can create strong verbal existence for characters (Balzac, Proust). It may be unevenly dispersed among characters. Analyses or composition should track how idiolects, sociolects, dialect, archaisms, anglicisms, etc., function as character markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of character-style individuation (tic → personal style → stylized pastiche)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of individuation: (a) minimal connotative relationship (occasional slips/tics), (b) recurrent linguistic characteristic (a tic/social marker), (c) continuous personal style, (d) stylized/pastiche speech (hyperbolic imitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these levels when creating or analyzing characters. Stylized pastiche maximizes mimetic effect but risks caricature; mid-level recurrent markers often suffice for social/psychological characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of hyperbolic mimesis: circularity and disappearance of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme stylistic objectivization (perfect mimesis) may become circular—character 'quotes' itself—and paradoxically leads to the character's disappearance (speech becomes imitation or caricature rather than living psychology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware: too-perfect idiolects can annul character substance and create a self-referential text that points back to the author's pastiche. Use moderation or strategic limitations to prevent stylistic overdetermination from undermining psychological complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective / focalization: who sees vs who speaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between mood (point of view/focalization—'who sees?') and voice (the narrator's identity—'who speaks?') is essential; many theoretical classifications conflate these different questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts and writers must separate (a) focalization (internal/outer point of view, i.e., whose perception organizes narrative information) from (b) voice (whether narrator is protagonist, minor character, omniscient author, etc.). Failure to do so leads to conceptual confusion in classification and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typologies of narrative situation (be wary of conflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several typologies exist (e.g., Brooks & Warren's fourfold table; Stanzel's three narrative situations: auktorial, Ich, personale; Friedman's eight types distinguishing omniscient, first-person subtypes, selective-omniscient, objective/dramatic camera modes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typologies as heuristics but avoid treating voice distinctions as point-of-view distinctions. Note: vertical distinctions in some tables relate to point of view (internal/external), while horizontal distinctions often concern narrator identity (voice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical vs horizontal demarcation in focalization tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In classification tables (e.g., Brooks & Warren), the vertical axis typically demarcates point of view (inner/outer), while the horizontal axis bears on voice (who is the narrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying classificatory schemes, map which axis corresponds to focalization vs narrator identity to avoid misreading the narrative situation (e.g., no real difference in point of view between some ostensibly different categories).
